correctness.rationale: The exterior-to-circle reduction follows by applying maximum modulus to the scalar matrix coefficients of (z−1)(zI−T_q)^−1; its limit at infinity is I, whereas its norm at −1 exceeds 1 for every q<1. Independently, for 0<q<1 put x=(1−q)/|z−q| on the circle and let b=(sqrt(4+x²)+x)/2 be the triangular singular norm. Since x=b−1/b, q times the squared boundary objective is b²(1−x²)=5/4−(b²−3/2)². As x increases through [(1−q)/(1+q),1], b increases, so the optimal point is the endpoint or x=1/sqrt(6), with the stated transition. The endpoint produces the first branch (also directly valid at q=0); the interior produces sqrt(5)/(2sqrt(q)) and |z−1|²=5(1−q)²/q. At the transition this distance squared is 4 and its derivative in q is −5(q_*^−2−1). Since 4−|e^{iθ}−1|² is asymptotic to (π−θ)², this gives both the exponent and the coefficient of angular splitting. Norm convergence T_q→I and the identity resolvent give the stated jump. The exact replay is the completed-square identity above together with the circle relation in RESULT.md lines 64–71; verify_ritt.py was inspected but not run, and its numerical samples are not the continuum proof.

value.rationale: The pencil is the straight norm-convergent path from the two-dimensional nilpotent Jordan contraction to I. Its exact resolvent norm is a meaningful sharpness benchmark, not just a sample value: the computation locates where the worst resolvent direction leaves −1, quantifies its angular motion, and gives an explicit failure of continuity at I within contractions. Useful as a finite-dimensional test for resolvent-constant estimates, without claiming a general higher-dimensional classification.
